list.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (ASCIA) Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention is an update of the 2016 ASCIA guideline. This updated guideline provides recommendations specifically in relation to infant feeding for food allergy prevention.
METHODS
A review of the guideline began in 2024, informed by a systematic evidence review process and using the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research & Evaluation II (AGREE II) framework. Where evidence was lacking, a formal Delphi process was used to develop recommendations based on expert consensus. An Expert Writing Group comprising representation from ASCIA, the National Allergy Council, Allergy & Anaphylaxis Australia the National Allergy Centre of Excellence and the Centre for Food Allergy Research was established. Key stakeholder meetings were held.
RESULTS
A systematic review of evidence resulted in 16 recommendations: eight based on published evidence; eight based on expert consensus. ASCIA recommends: In Australia and New Zealand, infants should be introduced to solid foods when they are showing signs of developmental readiness. This is usually around 6 months and not before 4 months of age. Soon after infants have started solid foods, well cooked egg and appropriate forms of peanut are included in the infant's diet. Other common food allergens included in the family diet should be offered to the infant. Once introduced, common food allergens should be offered around once a week. Breastfeeding is encouraged, with no maternal dietary modifications. Breastmilk substitutes based on hydrolysed milk protein, soy or other proteins are not recommended for allergy prevention. Mild perioral rashes which appear around food consumption (redness or contact urticaria with no other symptoms of allergy) may not be a sign of an allergic reaction, and the food should be offered again.
CONCLUSION
Key changes from the 2016 ASCIA guideline include specific recommendations regarding the timing of peanut and egg introduction, alongside a recommendation regarding perioral rashes to support primary healthcare providers. These guidelines require ongoing review and updating as new evidence emerges.
list.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention.
list.journal: Clinical and experimental allergy : journal of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: The ASCIA 2024 guideline updates recommendations for infant feeding to prevent food allergies, emphasizing early introduction of peanuts and eggs, breastfeeding without dietary restrictions, and reassessing perioral rashes. It includes 16 recommendations based on evidence and expert consensus.

list.abstract: Rationale: In February 2024, omalizumab was approved to reduce immunoglobulin E-mediated food allergic reactions. Given its potential as a novel therapeutic option, we aimed to perform a meta-analysis comparing omalizumab with placebo in enhancing food tolerance among allergic children and adolescents. Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Central for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing omalizumab to placebo in pediatric patients aged 1 to 19 with food allergy. Outcomes of interest were tolerance to 2g of peanut, respiratory tract infection and urticaria. Statistical analysis was performed with Web Review Manager (RevMan Web). Heterogeneity was assessed with I2 statistics. (PROSPERO registration ID: CRD42024580124). Results: Between 59 studies full-text reviewed, 4 RCTs met the eligibility criteria, including 280 patients with median age of 8.9 years. Two studies utilized oral immunotherapy as an adjunctive treatment. Omalizumab was used to evaluate the increase in allergen threshold in 195 (69.6%) randomized patients. Compared to placebo, we found that omalizumab (RR 11.18; 95% CI 3.70-33.79; p < 0.0001) was significantly associated with better tolerance to 2g of peanut. There was no significant difference in the incidence of upper respiratory tract infection (RR 1.08; 95% CI 0.37-3.14; p = 0.89), while urticaria (RR 0.54; 95% CI 0.11-2.55; p = 0.44) was considerably higher in the placebo group. Conclusions: Omalizumab appears to increase allergen tolerance in pediatric patients with food allergies and may be considered as a strategy to reduce the health risks associated with accidental or intentional exposures.
list.title: Efficacy and Safety of Omalizumab for Increase Tolerance in Pediatric Patients with Food Allergy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
list.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: Omalizumab significantly improves peanut tolerance in pediatric food allergy patients, with no significant difference in respiratory infections but higher urticaria in placebo.

list.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Food allergies are common and are associated with substantial morbidity; the only approved treatment is oral immunotherapy for peanut allergy.
METHODS
In this trial, we assessed whether omalizumab, a monoclonal anti-IgE antibody, would be effective and safe as monotherapy in patients with multiple food allergies. Persons 1 to 55 years of age who were allergic to peanuts and at least two other trial-specified foods (cashew, milk, egg, walnut, wheat, and hazelnut) were screened. Inclusion required a reaction to a food challenge of 100 mg or less of peanut protein and 300 mg or less of the two other foods. Participants were randomly assigned, in a 2:1 ratio, to receive omalizumab or placebo administered subcutaneously (with the dose based on weight and IgE levels) every 2 to 4 weeks for 16 to 20 weeks, after which the challenges were repeated. The primary end point was ingestion of peanut protein in a single dose of 600 mg or more without dose-limiting symptoms. The three key secondary end points were the consumption of cashew, of milk, and of egg in single doses of at least 1000 mg each without dose-limiting symptoms. The first 60 participants (59 of whom were children or adolescents) who completed this first stage were enrolled in a 24-week open-label extension.
RESULTS
Of the 462 persons who were screened, 180 underwent randomization. The analysis population consisted of the 177 children and adolescents (1 to 17 years of age). A total of 79 of the 118 participants (67%) receiving omalizumab met the primary end-point criteria, as compared with 4 of the 59 participants (7%) receiving placebo (P<0.001). Results for the key secondary end points were consistent with those of the primary end point (cashew, 41% vs. 3%; milk, 66% vs. 10%; egg, 67% vs. 0%; P<0.001 for all comparisons). Safety end points did not differ between the groups, aside from more injection-site reactions in the omalizumab group.
CONCLUSIONS
In persons as young as 1 year of age with multiple food allergies, omalizumab treatment for 16 weeks was superior to placebo in increasing the reaction threshold for peanut and other common food allergens. (Funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and others; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03881696.).
list.title: Omalizumab for the Treatment of Multiple Food Allergies.
list.journal: The New England journal of medicine
list.aiSummary: Omalizumab, a monoclonal anti-IgE antibody, demonstrated significant improvements in ingestion of peanut protein and other common food allergens in patients with multiple food allergies, when compared to placebo, without increasing safety end points. The study included patients aged 1 to 55 years, mostly children or adolescents.

list.abstract: Rationale: To evaluate oral mucosal immunotherapy (OMIT) as a new and innovative delivery system for allergen immunotherapy. Food allergy desensitization is achieved through an easy-to-use innovative technology, where the allergen is stabilized and embedded in a fully functional toothpaste, measured with a metered dose dispenser, and administered once daily. In the treatment of food allergy, we hypothesized that this pathway interacts with Langerhans cells in the entire oral cavity to activate an immune response, leading to allergen desensitization. Methods: Immunologic parameters were utilized to assist in diagnosing and evaluating the effectiveness of this new delivery system in 32 adult subjects with physician diagnosed food allergy. In addition to oral food challenges (OFC), biomarkers were assessed including Ara h 2, 3, 6, 8 & 9, to help confirm the diagnosis of peanut food allergy. Results: There was excellent correlation with Ara h 2 level of ≥1.75 kU/L and a positive OFC. In addition, there was a statistically significant increase in IgG4 and a decrease in IgE/IgG4 ratio in subjects who could tolerate ≥300mg peanut protein at end of study. However, one subject who failed the entry OFC had insignificant levels of Ara h 2, a negative skin prick test, positive Ara h 8 & 9, consistent with oral allergy syndrome. Consequently, there may be difficulty with the interpretation of OFCs in individuals presenting with oral allergy syndrome. Conclusions: Our data support OMIT as a new effective approach to the management of food allergy providing a robust immunologic response in treated patients.
list.title: First Study To Evaluate Oral Mucosal Immunotherapy (OMIT) For The Treatment of Food Allergy
list.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: The study evaluated the effectiveness of oral mucosal immunotherapy (OMIT) in treating food allergies, using a novel toothpaste-based delivery system. The therapy showed a positive correlation with Ara h 2 levels for diagnosis and increased IgG4 and decreased IgE/IgG4 ratio in subjects able to tolerate peanut protein. However, individuals with oral allergy syndrome may face challenges in OFC interpretation. This suggests OMIT as a promising new approach for food allergy management.

list.title: A Pragmatic, Open-label Study of Peanut Oral Immunotherapy in Inducing Desensitisation or Remission in Children With Food Allergy Compared to Standard Care (Strict Allergen Avoidance)
list.aiSummary: Peanut oral immunotherapy in children with food allergy may induce desensitisation or remission, offering a potential alternative to strict allergen avoidance. This pragmatic open-label study compares immunotherapy against standard care to assess long-term efficacy and safety outcomes.

list.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Clinical studies supported by immunological data indicate early life intervention strategies to be promising in reducing the growing global burden of food allergies. The events that predispose to food allergy, including the induction of allergen-specific immune responses, appear to be initiated early in development. Early exposure to food allergens in utero and via breast milk is likely to be important in initiating oral tolerance. We aim to determine the effectiveness of higher maternal food allergen consumption during pregnancy and lactation on infant food allergy outcomes.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS
This is a multisite, parallel, two-arm (1:1 allocation), single-blinded (outcome assessors, statistical analyst and investigators), randomised controlled trial. Pregnant women (<23 weeks' gestation) whose (unborn) infants have at least two biological family members (mother, father or siblings) with medically diagnosed allergic disease are eligible to participate. After obtaining written informed consent, pregnant women are randomised to either a high egg and peanut diet (at least 6 eggs and 60 peanuts per week) or standard (low) egg and peanut diet (no more than 3 eggs and 30 peanuts per week). The women are asked to follow their allocated diet from <23 weeks' gestation to 4 months' lactation. The primary outcome is food challenge proven IgE-mediated egg and/or peanut allergy in the infants at 12 months of age. Key secondary outcomes include infant sensitisation to egg and/or peanut and infant eczema. Our target sample size is 2136 women. Analyses will be performed on an intention-to-treat basis according to a pre-specified statistical analysis plan.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
Ethical approval has been granted from the Women's and Children's Health Network Human Research Ethics Committee (approval number HREC/18/WCHN/42). Trial results will be presented at scientific conferences and published in peer-reviewed journals.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12618000937213.
list.title: PrEggNut Study: protocol for a randomised controlled trial investigating the effect of a maternal diet rich in eggs and peanuts from <23 weeks' gestation during pregnancy to 4 months' lactation on infant IgE-mediated egg and peanut allergy outcomes.
list.aiSummary: The PrEggNut Study is a multisite, randomised controlled trial investigating the effect of a maternal diet rich in eggs and peanuts during pregnancy and lactation on infant IgE-mediated egg and peanut allergy outcomes. The study targets a sample size of 2136 pregnant women, with results presented at scientific conferences and published in peer-reviewed journals.

list.abstract: Rationale: Globally, one-third of newborns are fed formula within the first three days of life. The unphysiologically high amounts of supplements reduce the amount of colostrum the newborn receives. Colostrum is rich in bioactives, which may be critical for healthy immune development. Therefore, we hypothesise that non-exclusive colostrum feeding significantly impacts infant allergy risk beyond cow's milk allergy. Methods: Feeding practice data were extracted from hospital records for 666 mother-infant dyads enrolled in the ORIGINS cohort (Australia), and neonates were categorised as exclusive colostrum fed (ECF) or non-exclusively colostrum fed (NECF). Food allergy at one year of age was defined by a positive skin prick test and a maternal-reported child's immediate reaction to the food. Results: The prevalence of NECF was 46%. Compared to ECF, NECF infants were more likely to develop an egg allergy [aOR (95% CI): 3.41 (1.10, 10.54)] or a peanut food allergy [aOR (95% CI): 5.66 (1.08, 29.82)] by 12-18 months. NECF infants with late introduction of allergens (> 7 Months) had the highest odds of developing egg [aOR (95% CI): 9.50 (2.29, 39.38)] or peanut [aOR (95% CI): 7.57 (1.35, 42.46)] allergy compared with ECF infants with early introduction of allergens(≤ 7 Months). Conclusions: This study shows an association of NECF with an increased risk of food allergies and compromised efficacy of food allergy prevention by early introduction of allergens in the infant diet. This observation may shift the paradigm where food allergy prevention benefits from promoting colostrum feeding.
list.title: Non- Exclusive Colostrum Feeding Is Associated With An Increased Risk Of Food Allergy In One-Year-Old-Children
list.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: Non-exclusive colostrum feeding in newborns is linked to a higher risk of food allergies, such as egg and peanut, especially when allergens are introduced late. This suggests promoting exclusive colostrum feeding may aid in preventing food allergies.

list.abstract: Rationale: Omalizumab was approved by the FDA for the treatment of food allergy (FA) in February, 2024. This study describes the characteristics of the first patients who initiated omalizumab for FA in a real-world clinical setting. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of the electronic medical records of patients who initiated omalizumab for FA between February, 2024 and August, 2024 at the Johns Hopkins pediatric allergy clinic. Results: We identified 102 patients who had initiated therapy, with a median age of 14 years (range: 13 months to 26 years). Fifty-five percent were male. Most were White (71%), non-Hispanic (93%), and had private insurance (95%). Tree nut (75%) and peanut (69%) allergies were most common, followed by egg (37%), sesame (30%), milk (29%), shellfish (13%), wheat (10%), soy (8%), and fish (8%). 26% had allergies to additional foods. 79% had multiple FAs, with a median of 3 FAs per patient (range: 1 to 7 FAs). Atopic comorbidities were common: 75% had a history of asthma or wheezing, 79% had atopic dermatitis, and 85% had environmental allergies. Conclusions: More than three quarters of Johns Hopkins patients who initiated omalizumab had multiple FAs, particularly to tree nuts and peanuts. The majority also had atopic comorbidities. The characteristics of the treatment population demonstrate that omalizumab was utilized to address multiple FAs and associated atopic conditions across a wide age range. Further work is needed to better understand nationwide uptake and utilization of this therapy.
list.title: Real-world Uptake of Omalizumab for Food Allergy
list.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: Omalizumab was used for multiple food allergies, especially tree nuts and peanuts, in a diverse group of patients with common atopic comorbidities at Johns Hopkins. The study highlights the real-world application and characteristics of omalizumab use for food allergies.

list.abstract: Rationale: Diagnosing food allergy (FA) in the infant population is challenging due to the overlap of symptoms between IgE- and non-IgE-mediated FA. The aim of this study is to better understand the manifestations of IgE and non-IgE mediated FA in infancy. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study to identify all infants ages 0 to 12 months who presented with FA concerns at the Pediatric Allergy Clinic of the University of Rochester Medical Center between January 2014 and January 2024. Seventeen symptoms related to stool, behavior, skin, and gastrointestinal concerns were analyzed. Results: Our preliminary data identified 500 infants diagnosed with FA. The median age of initial presentation was 7 months; 60% male, 73% white 16% Black/African American, and 5% Asian. The most prevalent presenting symptoms were rash (26%) followed by vomiting (25%), and atopic dermatitis (24%). Initial visit diagnoses included: no FA (60%), IgE-mediated FA (27%), food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP) (9%), and food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) (8%). The most prevalent food triggers in both groups were egg (21%), peanut (14%), and milk (12%). Food allergy was outgrown in 18% of patients during an average follow-up of 31 months. Conclusions: Our preliminary findings highlight a greater prevalence of IgE-mediated FA (27%) compared to non-IgE-mediated FA (17%), with egg, peanut, and milk as the most common triggers. Notably, skin and GI symptoms were the most frequent presenting manifestations. Through continued chart review, this analysis aims to further elucidate the early manifestations of FA, assess possible overlap, and refine our preliminary results.
list.title: Distribution of IgE and Non-IgE Mediated Food Allergies
list.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: The study found that IgE-mediated food allergies are more common than non-IgE types in infants, with egg, peanut, and milk as primary triggers, and skin and gastrointestinal symptoms being the most frequent presentations.

list.abstract: Rationale: Comorbid IgE-mediated food allergy in pediatric food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) was reported to be as high as 65% in a 2015 national survey. The prevalence of comorbid non-IgE-mediated food allergies, such as eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders (EGIDs) and food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP) remains unknown. Our study aimed to examine the incidence and characteristics of comorbid IgE and non-IgE-mediated food allergies in a large multicenter cohort of pediatric FPIES patients in the Southwestern United States. Methods: We queried a multicenter clinical pediatric FPIES registry in order to collect data on incidence and characteristics of comorbid IgE-mediated food allergies, EGIDs and FPIAP. Descriptive statistics were conducted. Results: Comorbid IgE-mediated food allergy was reported in 18.6% (n=177) of the total FPIES patient cohort (n=952). The most common IgE-mediated allergens were egg (10.2%; n=97), peanut (7.8%; n=75), and cow’s milk (6%; n=57). FPIAP was seen in 7.1% (n=68) of FPIES patients. [AS1] Patients with non-milk FPIES were more likely to have milk FPIAP than patients with milk FPIES (7.4% vs 0.6%; n=58 vs n=1). Comorbid EGIDs were seen in 1.8% (n=17) of FPIES patients; of those, all but one patient had eosinophilic esophagitis. Soy was the most common FPIES trigger associated with comorbid EGIDs (41%; n=7). Conclusions: In the largest multi-center FPIES registry to date, findings provide additional evidence on the prevalence of comorbid IgE (18.6%) and non-IgE-mediated food allergies. Understanding the complex, often overlapping clinical presentations of FPIES and other immune-mediated food reactions can improve diagnosis, management, and health outcomes.
list.title: Food Allergy Comorbidities in a Multicenter FPIES Cohort
list.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
list.aiSummary: In a large multicenter FPIES cohort, 18.6% had comorbid IgE-mediated allergies, while 7.1% had FPIAP and 1.8% had EGIDs, highlighting the prevalence of comorbid food allergies in pediatric FPIES patients.
